<action type="say">
You’ve done the most important part. Now it’s mainly cleanup and monitoring. Here’s what I’d do next:

1) Watch for any weird transactions  
- Check **recent activity daily** for the next week or two.  
- Anything you don’t recognize: use the app’s **dispute/“Report a problem”** option or call support and tell them this was after the card was reported lost.

2) Turn on strong alerts (if not already)  
In the app, under **Alerts/Notifications**:  
- Enable **transaction alerts for all purchases** (or at least for card-not-present/online and international).  
- Turn on alerts for **card declines** too, so you know if a lost-card transaction is being attempted.

3) Recurring payments & subscriptions  
Once your **new card number is active**, you’ll need to update any place that auto-charges this card. Typical ones:  
- Cloud/IT SaaS tools (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Adobe, AWS, etc.)  
- Software subscriptions (Slack, Zoom, Dropbox, Atlassian, password managers, etc.)  
- Online services (domains/hosting, marketing tools, analytics, CRM, payroll, etc.)  
- Utilities or services (phone/internet, insurance, streaming, etc.)

Some merchants automatically get the new card via **account updater** services, but you **cannot rely on that**. Plan on doing a quick sweep and updating key vendors once the new card arrives.

4) Card-on-file risk check  
Think of any places you’ve saved this card for **one-click checkout**:  
- Large marketplaces (Amazon, eBay, etc.)  
- Food delivery / rideshare / travel apps  
If there’s any app/service you don’t use anymore or don’t fully trust, remove this card from their payment methods when you add the new one, or don’t add it back at all.

5) Upcoming charges you can’t miss  
- List any **critical upcoming payments** that would have hit this card in the next 1–2 weeks (e.g., vendor bills, renewals).  
- For anything urgent, temporarily switch to another card or arrange a different payment method until the new card arrives, so nothing gets canceled for non-payment.

6) If you find the old card later  
- Do **not** try to use it.  
- Destroy it (cut through the chip and magnetic stripe).

If you want, tell me what you mainly use this card for (e.g., “business SaaS + travel”, or “general online spend”), and I can help you build a quick checklist of the most likely merchants and subscriptions to update when the replacement shows up. </action>

<think>

<action type="say">
Here’s a condensed checklist you can keep handy for when the new card arrives. Focus on anything marked “often forgotten”:

1) Core business + SaaS tools  
- Productivity: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Adobe, Zoom  
- Collaboration: Slack, Dropbox/Box, Notion, Asana, Monday, Trello  
- Dev/infra: AWS, Azure, GCP, GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare  
- CRM/marketing: Salesforce/HubSpot/Pipedrive, Mailchimp, SendGrid, Twilio, Stripe/PayPal billing  
- Accounting: QuickBooks/Xero/FreshBooks (subscription + any auto-billed services)

2) Domains, hosting, and web stack (often forgotten)  
- Domain registrars: GoDaddy, Namecheap, Google Domains, etc.  
- Web hosting: WP Engine, Squarespace, Wix, Shopify, Webflow, custom VPS providers  
- SSL / security tools: any certificate or security service that auto-renews.

3) Communications + utilities  
- Business phone/VoIP: RingCentral, Zoom Phone, Google Voice, etc.  
- Internet and mobile service (if billed to this card)  
- Video conferencing / webinar tools beyond your main ones.

4) Finance + recurring vendor payments  
- Other SaaS that invoices monthly/annually and auto-charges this card  
- Any “usage-based” tools (API usage, SMS gateways like Twilio, email APIs, etc.).  

5) Travel & transportation  
- Airlines/hotels with stored cards in your profile  
- Travel booking tools (Concur, Navan, etc.)  
- Rideshare and delivery apps used for work (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, etc.).

6) General online / personal services (often forgotten)  
- Cloud storage: iCloud, Google One, OneDrive (if on separate personal accounts)  
- Streaming or news subscriptions you actually need for work or generally: Netflix, Spotify, major newspapers, industry journals  
- App store subscriptions (Apple App Store / Google Play) tied to this card.

7) Risk and convenience clean-up  
When you update to the new card, use it as a tidy-up moment:  
- Remove the card from any services you **don’t plan to use again**.  
- For anything you barely remember signing up for, consider canceling rather than updating.

Practical way to not miss anything:  
- When the new card arrives and is active, check the **last 2–3 statements** for that old card and make a short list of any merchant that bills you regularly (monthly/quarterly/annually). Those are the must-update ones.

If you’d like, you can paste a redacted list of a few recent statement line items (just merchant names, no amounts/card numbers), and I can help you mark which ones almost certainly need updating. </action>
